title: One counterexample is enough
objectives: Disprove a general claim with a single counterexample, and tell when an example proves nothing.

screens.title: A prime machine
screens.prose: Claim: $n^2 + n + 41$ is prime for every whole number $n \ge 0$. Test the first few cases.
screens.question: Work out $n^2 + n + 41$ for each $n$.

feedback.correct: Right. 41, 43, 47, 53, 61 and 71, and every one is prime.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Square $n$, add $n$, then add 41.

explain.text: The values are 41, 43, 47, 53, 61 and 71. Each one is prime. The pattern looks strong.

screens.title: Case 40
screens.prose: In fact every value from $n = 0$ up to $n = 39$ is prime. Forty cases in a row. Now try $n = 40$.
screens.question: Work out $40^2 + 40 + 41$.

byKey.non: You left out the $+n$ term: $1600 + 41$. Add the 40 as well.

explain.text: $40^2 + 40 + 41 = 40 \times 41 + 41 = 41 \times 41 = 1681$. So 1681 is not prime. Forty true cases, and the claim is still false.

screens.title: One case is enough
screens.prose:
A "for all" claim is false as soon as one case fails. From Saying the opposite:

$$\lnot\, \forall n\ P(n) \;\equiv\; \exists n\ \lnot P(n)$$

The failing case is a **counterexample**. Here $n = 40$ is one.
screens.question: How many failing cases does it take to refute a "for all" claim?

options.text: At least two, to rule out a fluke
options.why: You asked for a second case. One checked failure is not a fluke: the claim said every case.

options.text: More than the number of cases that pass
options.why: You weighed cases against each other. Forty passes do not outvote one failure.

options.text: None: a "for all" claim can only be checked, never refuted
options.why: It can be refuted. $n = 40$ just did it.

feedback.correct: Right. One counterexample refutes a "for all" claim.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The claim says every case works, so one failure breaks it.

explain.text: "For every $n$" fails exactly when some $n$ fails. One checked case, $n = 40$, establishes that. No number of passing cases can outweigh it.

screens.title: The first odd failure
screens.prose: Claim: every odd number greater than 1 is prime. It holds for 3, 5 and 7.
screens.question: Tap the smallest counterexample.

hints.text: Look for an odd number with a factor other than 1 and itself.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the first odd number in the list that has a factor.

byKey.r2c2: 15 is a counterexample, but a smaller one comes first.
byKey.r2c5: 21 is a counterexample, but a smaller one comes first.
byKey.r1c5: 11 is prime, so it agrees with the claim.

explain.text: 9 is odd, greater than 1, and equals $3 \times 3$. So it refutes the claim. 15 and 21 would do too, but one is enough.

screens.title: Squaring a sum
screens.prose: Claim: $(a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2$ for all real $a$ and $b$. The shaded squares are $a^2 + b^2$.
screens.question: Which pairs are counterexamples? Select all that apply.

options.why: Both sides are 25 here, so the claim holds for this pair.
Both sides are 0 here, so the claim holds for this pair.

hints.text: Work out both sides for each pair.

feedback.correct: Right. $(1, 1)$ gives 4 against 2, and $(2, 3)$ gives 25 against 13.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute both sides for each pair.

explain.text: The square has two unshaded $ab$ pieces, so $(a + b)^2 = a^2 + 2ab + b^2$. The claim fails whenever $ab \ne 0$. With a zero, as in $(0, 5)$, it happens to hold.

screens.title: Irrational plus irrational
screens.prose: Claim: if $a$ and $b$ are irrational then $a + b$ is irrational. Contradiction showed $\sqrt{2}$ is irrational.
screens.question: Which pair is a counterexample?

options.why: $\sqrt{2} + \sqrt{2} = 2\sqrt{2}$, which is irrational. That pair agrees with the claim.
1 is rational, so the hypothesis fails. A counterexample needs both irrational.

options.text: None exists: the claim is true
options.why: Look for two irrationals whose irrational parts cancel.

hints.text: A counterexample needs both numbers irrational and the sum rational.

feedback.correct: Right. Both irrational, and the sum is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find two irrationals with a rational sum.

byKey.one: You used 1, which is rational. The hypothesis must hold before the conclusion can fail.

explain.text: $\sqrt{2}$ and $-\sqrt{2}$ are both irrational. Their sum is 0, which is rational. So the claim is false.

screens.title: Four primes, then
screens.prose: Claim: $2^p - 1$ is prime whenever $p$ is prime. It holds for $p = 2, 3, 5, 7$. Next is $p = 11$, with $2^{11} - 1 = 2047$, and 23 divides it.
screens.question: What is $2047 \div 23$?

byKey.n: You gave 2047 itself. Divide it by 23.

explain.text: $23 \times 89 = 2047$, so $2^{11} - 1$ is not prime. Since 11 is prime, the hypothesis holds and the conclusion fails. Four confirming cases did not make the claim true.

screens.title: Refuting an implication
screens.prose: Claim: if $n$ is prime then $n$ is odd. As in If, then, an implication breaks only where $P$ holds and $Q$ fails.
screens.question: Which number is a counterexample?

options.why: 9 is odd and not prime. The hypothesis fails, so 9 refutes nothing.
1 is not prime, so the hypothesis fails. It cannot break the rule.
3 is prime and odd. It agrees with the claim.

hints.text: A counterexample must make the hypothesis true.
So it must be prime, and then not odd.

feedback.correct: Right. 2 is prime and not odd.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look in the region where $P$ holds and $Q$ fails.

byKey.nine: You picked a number that is not prime. A counterexample to $P \Rightarrow Q$ needs $P$ true and $Q$ false.
byKey.one: You picked 1, which is not prime. Only primes can test this claim.

explain.text: $P \Rightarrow Q$ fails only in region A: $P$ true, $Q$ false. The only number there is 2. 9 is a counterexample to a different claim, that every odd number is prime.

screens.title: Searching in code
screens.prose: A search finds counterexamples quickly. A search that finds none is evidence, not proof. `is_prime(m)` is defined for you; numbers below 2 are not prime.
screens.question: Write `first_failure(f, n_max)`. It returns the smallest $n$ from 0 to `n_max` where `f(n)` is not prime. If there is none, it returns `None`.

widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests. Each defines `f` in one line and expects a whole number or `None`.

hints.text: Loop `n` over `range(n_max + 1)`, so that `n_max` itself is checked.
Return `n` as soon as `not is_prime(f(n))`. After the loop, return `None`.

feedback.correct: Your search finds 40 for $n^2 + n + 41$ and 41 for $n^2 - n + 41$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the first failing test: did your loop start at 0 and reach `n_max`?

byKey.test-5: $0^2 + 1 = 1$, and 1 is not prime, so the answer is 0. Start the loop at 0.

explain.text:
The loop tests $n = 0, 1, \dots$ and stops at the first failure. With `n_max` 39 it finds nothing for $n^2 + n + 41$, which proves nothing. With `n_max` 100 it finds 40.

```python
for n in range(n_max + 1):
    if not is_prime(f(n)):
        return n
return None
```

screens.title: Writing it up
screens.prose: A counterexample, written so a stranger can check it: state the claim, give the case, check the hypothesis, check the conclusion fails, and conclude.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Claim: for every prime $p$, $2^p - 1$ is prime.
11 is prime, so the hypothesis holds.
$p = 2, 3, 5, 7$ all give primes, so the claim is probably true.
lines.why: You argued from confirming cases. They cannot outweigh one failure.

hints.text: Then name the case and check both halves of the implication.
Claim; $p = 11$; hypothesis holds; conclusion fails; false.

feedback.correct: Right. Claim, case, hypothesis true, conclusion false, verdict.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. State the claim, name the case, then check the hypothesis before the conclusion.

byKey.d1: You kept the confirming cases. They are not part of a refutation.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line. A reader needs both the hypothesis check and the conclusion check.

explain.text: Each line gives the reader one thing to check. The hypothesis check matters: without it, 9 might be offered for a claim about primes. The factorisation $23 \times 89$ lets anyone confirm the failure.

screens.title: A positive return that hurts
screens.prose: Claim: adding a stock with a positive average return always raises a portfolio's average return. A portfolio averages 8% a year. Half of it is moved into a stock averaging 5%.
screens.question: What is the new portfolio's average return?

hints.text: The new average is a weighted average.

feedback.correct: Right. 6.5%, down from 8%: a counterexample to "always".
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each return by its half.

byKey.sum: You added the two returns. Weight each by 50%.
byKey.five: You gave the new stock's return alone. Half the portfolio still earns 8%.
byKey.eight: You left the portfolio unchanged. Half of it now earns 5%.

explain.text: $0.5 \times 8\% + 0.5 \times 5\% = 6.5\%$, below 8%. So one case refutes "always". A claim that something usually helps is tested with data, not refuted by one case.

ideas: A "for all" claim is false as soon as one case fails, since $\lnot \forall$ is $\exists \lnot$.
No number of confirming cases proves a "for all" claim: $n^2 + n + 41$ is prime for 40 cases, then fails.
A counterexample to $P \Rightarrow Q$ must make $P$ true and $Q$ false. One example does prove an $\exists$ claim.

formula.name: Counterexample
formula.note: One checked failing case refutes the claim.

summary.trap: To refute "if prime then odd", 9 does nothing: it is not prime. The counterexample is 2.

quiz.prose: "Adding a stock with a positive average return **always** raises a portfolio's average return." The 8% portfolio fell to 6.5%.
quiz.question: Which word in the claim does the counterexample kill?

options.why: The new stock's return was positive, 5%. That part of the claim held.
Average returns are what we computed. The claim's error is how widely it applies.
"Raises" is fine for some stocks, such as one averaging 10%. The claim fails because of "always".

feedback.correct: Right. One case shows it does not always happen.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which word made the claim cover every case.

explain.text: "Always" makes it a "for all" claim, which one case refutes. A stock above 8% would raise the average. So the true statement depends on the stock.

quiz.prose: Claim: some even number is prime.
quiz.question: Which proves it?

options.why: That is about odd primes. It does not show an even prime exists.
That shows some even number is not prime. It says nothing about primes.

options.text: No even prime exists up to 100 except one, so it is likely.
options.why: You argued from a search. One example, named and checked, proves an "exists" claim.

feedback.correct: Right. One example proves a "there exists" claim.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A "there exists" claim needs one example that works.

explain.text: "Some even number is prime" is an $\exists$ claim. The example 2 proves it outright. This is the one time a single example proves something.

quiz.question: Which of these claims does $n = 9$ refute? Select all that apply.

options.text: Every odd number greater than 1 is prime.
If $n$ is odd then $n^2$ is odd.
options.why: 9 is odd and $81$ is odd. It agrees with the claim.
9 is a multiple of 3 and odd, so it agrees. 6 would refute it.

feedback.correct: Right. 9 is odd and not prime, and a square that is odd.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each claim, check that 9 meets the hypothesis and fails the conclusion.

explain.text: 9 is odd, above 1 and $3 \times 3$, so it refutes the first claim. It is the square $3^2$ and odd, so it refutes the second. The other two hold at 9.

quiz.prose: The next failure of $n^2 + n + 41$ is at $n = 41$, where the value is $1763$.
quiz.question: What is $1763 \div 41$?

byKey.41: You gave the divisor. Divide 1763 by 41.

explain.text: $41^2 + 41 + 41 = 41 \times 43 = 1763$. So $n = 41$ fails as well. Forty passes in a row can still hide a false claim.
